about: LAWS0006 is UCL Laws' compulsory 30-credit first-year module on UK constitutional and administrative law, taught in person across Terms 1 and 2 and assessed in 2026/27 by a 100% examination. Part 1 covers Parliament, the Cabinet and central executive powers, devolved legislatures and governments, and constitutional principles (separation of powers, the rule of law, accountability and legislative supremacy). Part 2 covers judicial review, the constitutional dimensions of the UK-EU relationship, and human rights under the Human Rights Act 1998, with Brexit, the rise of the common law constitution and recent parliamentary reforms running through the module. This pack adds a short opening topic on constitutional sources.
topics: The UK constitution: sources, conventions and the common law
Parliament, the Cabinet and the powers of central government
Separation of powers and the rule of law
Legislative supremacy of Parliament and parliamentary accountability
The UK-EU constitutional relationship and Brexit
Human rights protection under the Human Rights Act 1998

notes.body:
The UK has no single codified constitution. Its constitutional rules come from several sources, and much of the module asks how these sources fit together and who should have the final say.

Statute
Acts of Parliament are the highest source of law. Some have special constitutional importance, for example Magna Carta 1297 (parts still in force), the Bill of Rights 1689, the Acts of Union 1706-07 and 1800, the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949, the European Communities Act 1972 (repealed), the Human Rights Act 1998, the devolution Acts of 1998, the Constitutional Reform Act 2005 and the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018.

"Constitutional statutes"
In Thoburn v Sunderland City Council [2002] EWHC 195 (Admin), Laws LJ suggested that "constitutional statutes" cannot be impliedly repealed by later Acts, only by express words or words so specific that the inference of actual intention is irresistible. In R (HS2 Action Alliance) v Secretary of State for Transport [2014] UKSC 3, Lords Neuberger and Mance (obiter) recognised "constitutional instruments" and suggested that even EU law might not automatically override fundamental principles in them, such as Article 9 of the Bill of Rights.

The common law
The courts have long protected basic rights and principles through the common law, for example in Entick v Carrington (1765), where a search of a writer's home under a warrant issued by a minister was held unlawful because no law authorised it. A theme of the module is the "rise of the common law" as a source of constitutional protection:
- The principle of legality: fundamental rights cannot be overridden by general or ambiguous words (R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex p Simms [2000] 2 AC 115).
- Access to the courts: in R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor [2017] UKSC 51, employment tribunal fees were unlawful because they effectively prevented people from enforcing their rights.
- Limits on ouster clauses (Anisminic v Foreign Compensation Commission [1969] 2 AC 147; R (Privacy International) v Investigatory Powers Tribunal [2019] UKSC 22).
- Limits on the prerogative (R (Miller) v Secretary of State for Exiting the EU [2017] UKSC 5; R (Miller) v Prime Minister [2019] UKSC 41).

Constitutional conventions
Conventions are binding political rules that the courts do not enforce directly. Examples include:
- the monarch gives Royal Assent to Bills passed by Parliament and appoints as Prime Minister the person able to command the confidence of the Commons;
- collective and individual ministerial responsibility;
- the Sewel convention on legislating in devolved areas.
The courts can recognise conventions, but not enforce them: Attorney-General v Jonathan Cape [1976] QB 752 (the Crossman diaries, where the court relied on the law of confidence instead) and Miller I (the Sewel convention is not legally enforceable). In Madzimbamuto v Lardner-Burke [1969] 1 AC 645, a convention that the UK Parliament would not legislate for Southern Rhodesia without its consent did not limit Parliament's legal power.

Other sources
- The royal prerogative: the residue of the Crown's common law powers.
- Parliamentary law and custom (the law and practice of Parliament).
- Soft law, such as the Ministerial Code and the Cabinet Manual.
- International obligations, which bind the UK internationally but are not part of domestic law unless incorporated by statute (the dualist approach).

Debate: should the UK codify?
Supporters of a written constitution point to clarity, entrenched rights and limits on executive power. Opponents value flexibility and democratic control by Parliament, and fear that it would hand political questions to judges.

Exam tips: When discussing any constitutional question, identify which source is involved (statute, common law, prerogative or convention) and whether it is legally enforceable. Recent cases on common law constitutional rights are essential evidence for essays on the changing UK constitution.

notes.h: Parliament, the Cabinet and the powers of central government
notes.body:
Parliament
- The House of Commons is elected and is the dominant chamber. The government is formed from the party (or parties) that can command its confidence.
- The House of Lords is unelected. After the House of Lords Act 1999 removed most hereditary peers, 92 remained. The House of Lords (Hereditary Peers) Act 2026 (Royal Assent 18 March 2026) removed those remaining, with effect from the end of the parliamentary session on 29 April 2026; hereditary peers who also hold life peerages can still sit. At the time of writing (October 2026), the Lords is made up mainly of life peers and bishops; check for further reform.
- The Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 allow most public Bills to become law without the Lords' consent after a delay of about a year (one month for money Bills). They cannot be used to extend the life of Parliament beyond five years. The Salisbury convention means the Lords does not block government Bills implementing manifesto commitments.
- Parliament's functions include legislating, scrutinising and holding the government to account (questions, debates, select committees) and approving taxation and spending.

The executive: Prime Minister and Cabinet
- The Prime Minister is appointed by the monarch by convention as the person most able to command the confidence of the Commons. The office is largely governed by convention.
- Collective ministerial responsibility: ministers publicly support Cabinet decisions or resign, and Cabinet discussions are confidential. The government must resign or seek a dissolution if it loses a confidence vote.
- Individual ministerial responsibility: ministers are accountable to Parliament for their departments and must not knowingly mislead Parliament. The Ministerial Code sets out expectations, but resignations for departmental failures are rare.
- Civil servants are politically impartial; the civil service is now on a statutory footing (Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010, Part 1).

Sources of executive power
- Statute: most government powers come from Acts of Parliament, often with wide powers to make delegated legislation (statutory instruments). "Henry VIII powers", which allow ministers to amend Acts by secondary legislation, are controversial.
- The royal prerogative: the residue of discretionary powers left in the Crown, now mostly exercised by ministers. It includes making treaties, conducting foreign affairs, deploying the armed forces, the prerogative of mercy, granting honours and proroguing Parliament (still a prerogative power, as Miller II shows); since 2022 the power to dissolve Parliament is again a prerogative power (see below).

Legal limits on the prerogative
- The Case of Proclamations (1611): the King cannot change the law by proclamation.
- No new prerogatives can be created (BBC v Johns [1965] Ch 32).
- Where statute covers the same ground, the prerogative is displaced (Attorney-General v De Keyser's Royal Hotel [1920] AC 508), and ministers cannot use the prerogative to frustrate a statutory scheme (R v Home Secretary, ex p Fire Brigades Union [1995] 2 AC 513).
- The exercise of prerogative powers can be judicially reviewed, depending on the subject matter (Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service (GCHQ) [1985] AC 374). Some matters, such as national security, are less suitable for review.
- The prerogative cannot be used to change domestic law or remove rights created by Parliament (Miller I [2017]).
- Statute increasingly controls the prerogative: for example, treaties must normally be laid before Parliament for 21 sitting days before ratification (Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010, s20).

Dissolution: recent reform
- The Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011 removed the prerogative power to dissolve Parliament and allowed early elections only in limited cases.
- The Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022 repealed the 2011 Act (s1) and revived the prerogative powers to dissolve Parliament and call a new one (s2). Section 3 provides that courts may not question the exercise of these powers, any decision relating to them, or their limits or extent. If not dissolved earlier, Parliament dissolves automatically five years after the day it first met (s4).

Exam tips: When asked about executive power, identify its source (statute or prerogative), then discuss legal limits (courts) and political limits (Parliament and conventions). Use recent reforms, such as the 2022 and 2026 Acts, to show how the balance is changing.

Since 1998, power has been devolved to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Devolution is asymmetric: each settlement is different, and England has no parliament of its own.

Scotland
- Scotland Act 1998: the Scottish Parliament can make laws (Acts of the Scottish Parliament) on all matters except those reserved to Westminster in Schedule 5 (e.g. the constitution, the Union, foreign affairs, defence) or protected from modification by Schedule 4 (including the Human Rights Act 1998 and much of the Scotland Act itself).
- A provision is outside legislative competence if, among other things, it relates to reserved matters or is incompatible with Convention rights (s29). Such a provision is not law.
- Section 28(7): devolution does not affect the power of the UK Parliament to make laws for Scotland.
- Scotland Act 2016: s28(8) records that the UK Parliament "will not normally" legislate on devolved matters without the Scottish Parliament's consent (the Sewel convention), and s63A states that the Scottish Parliament and Government are a permanent part of the UK's constitutional arrangements, not to be abolished without a referendum in Scotland.

Wales
- Devolution began with executive powers in 1998. The Government of Wales Act 2006 separated the Welsh Government from the Assembly and let the Assembly pass Measures; after a 2011 referendum it gained power to pass Acts on devolved subjects. The Wales Act 2017 moved Wales to a reserved powers model like Scotland's.
- The Assembly was renamed Senedd Cymru (Welsh Parliament) in 2020. From the May 2026 election, the Senedd has 96 members, elected by closed-list proportional representation in 16 six-member constituencies, with four-year terms.

Northern Ireland
- The Northern Ireland Act 1998 implemented the Belfast (Good Friday) Agreement 1998. Power-sharing between the main communities is required in the Executive. Matters are excepted (never devolved), reserved (may be devolved) or transferred.
- The institutions have been suspended several times; most recently they were restored in February 2024.

England
There is no English parliament. Devolution within England takes the form of combined authorities and elected mayors. The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 created a framework of "strategic authorities" with defined areas of competence.

The Sewel convention and the courts
- Miller I [2017] UKSC 5: the Sewel convention is a political convention; its recognition in s28(8) did not make it legally enforceable, so the devolved legislatures had no legal veto over Brexit legislation.
- The UK Parliament has since legislated without consent several times, notably the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018.

Supreme Court references on competence
- AXA General Insurance v HM Advocate [2011] UKSC 46: Acts of the Scottish Parliament can be judicially reviewed at common law only on extreme grounds related to the rule of law, not for irrationality.
- UK Withdrawal from the EU (Legal Continuity) (Scotland) Bill Reference [2018] UKSC 64: the Bill as a whole was within competence, but a provision requiring the Scottish Ministers' consent to certain UK ministerial regulations was outside competence because it would have modified s28(7). Many other provisions became outside competence because the later UK Act was protected from modification.
- UNCRC (Incorporation) (Scotland) Bill Reference [2021] UKSC 42: several provisions were outside competence because they would have restricted the UK Parliament's power to legislate for Scotland, modifying s28(7).
- Scottish Independence Referendum Bill Reference [2022] UKSC 31: a Bill for an independence referendum related to the reserved matters of the Union and the UK Parliament, so it was outside competence, even though the referendum would be advisory.
- Re Allister [2023] UKSC 5: the Northern Ireland Protocol (now the Windsor Framework) was lawfully given effect by the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018, which modified the Acts of Union 1800 in relation to trade.

Exam tips: For "is it within competence?" problems, check reserved matters, Schedule 4 protections and Convention rights. For essays, contrast the legal position (Westminster sovereignty, s28(7)) with the political reality (permanence and the Sewel convention).

notes.h: Separation of powers and the rule of law
notes.body:
Separation of powers
The idea, associated with Montesquieu (The Spirit of the Laws, 1748), is that the legislative, executive and judicial functions should be distributed so that no single body can abuse power. The UK has only a partial separation:
- The executive sits in and usually controls the legislature (ministers must be MPs or peers), so the system is better described as a fusion of the legislature and executive, balanced by checks.
- The judiciary is now institutionally separate. The Constitutional Reform Act 2005 (CRA):
  - recognised the rule of law and the Lord Chancellor's existing role in relation to it (s1);
  - imposed a duty on ministers and others to uphold the continued independence of the judiciary, and barred ministers from seeking to influence judicial decisions through special access (s3);
  - made the Lord Chief Justice head of the judiciary of England and Wales (s7), removing the Lord Chancellor's judicial role;
  - created the Supreme Court (s23), which replaced the Appellate Committee of the House of Lords in 2009;
  - created the Judicial Appointments Commission (s61).
- Courts respect the role of Parliament: in Duport Steels v Sirs [1980] 1 WLR 142 Lord Diplock stressed that judges must apply statutes, not substitute their own policy views.
- The courts also check the executive: in M v Home Office [1994] 1 AC 377, a minister could be found in contempt of court in his official capacity.
- Judges should not exercise executive functions such as sentencing: in R (Anderson) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] UKHL 46, the Home Secretary's power to set minimum terms for murderers was declared incompatible with Article 6.

The rule of law
- Dicey (Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution, 1885) gave three meanings: no one is punishable except for a distinct breach of law established in the ordinary courts; everyone, including officials, is equal before the ordinary law; and the constitution results from judicial decisions on individual rights.
- Thin (formal) versions focus on the form of law: clear, prospective, public and stable rules (e.g. Raz). Thick (substantive) versions include respect for fundamental rights.
- Lord Bingham (The Rule of Law, 2010) set out eight principles, including that the law must be accessible, clear and predictable; questions of right should be resolved by law, not discretion; ministers must act within their powers, fairly and in good faith; the law must protect fundamental human rights; and the state must comply with its international obligations.

The rule of law in the courts
- Entick v Carrington (1765): officials need legal authority to interfere with the citizen.
- R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor [2017] UKSC 51: access to justice is a constitutional right.
- R (Evans) v Attorney General [2015] UKSC 21: the Upper Tribunal ordered disclosure of Prince Charles's letters to ministers under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. The Attorney General issued a certificate under s53 overriding the decision because he disagreed with it. The Supreme Court (5-2) held the certificate invalid, but the majority split on the reasoning. Lord Neuberger (with Lords Kerr and Reed) reasoned that allowing a member of the executive to override a judicial decision simply because he took a different view would offend two basic principles: that court decisions are binding and that executive action is reviewable by the courts. Clear words would be needed, and s53 did not contain them. Lord Mance (with Lady Hale) took a less strict view: a certificate could be issued after disagreeing with a tribunal, but only with very solid reasons, and this one did not properly engage with the tribunal's findings. Lords Wilson and Hughes dissented. (By 6-1, the certificate was also invalid as to environmental information, because of EU law.)
- Ouster clauses are read narrowly to preserve access to the courts (Anisminic [1969]; Privacy International [2019]).

Exam tips: Avoid treating separation of powers as absolute in the UK. Use the CRA 2005 to show formal separation of the judiciary, and Evans, UNISON and Miller II to show how the courts protect the rule of law against the executive.

notes.h: Legislative supremacy of Parliament and parliamentary accountability
notes.body:
The orthodox (Diceyan) view
Dicey said Parliament has "the right to make or unmake any law whatever", and that no person or body can override or set aside its legislation. Three consequences follow:
- Parliament can legislate on any subject (Mortensen v Peters (1906), a Scottish case where a statute prevailed over international law).
- Courts cannot question the validity of an Act or the procedure by which it was passed (the enrolled Act rule: Edinburgh and Dalkeith Railway v Wauchope (1842); British Railways Board v Pickin [1974] AC 765).
- Parliament cannot bind its successors: a later inconsistent Act impliedly repeals an earlier one (Vauxhall Estates v Liverpool Corporation [1932] 1 KB 733; Ellen Street Estates v Minister of Health [1934] 1 KB 590).

Challenges to the orthodox view
- Manner and form: some argue Parliament can bind its successors as to the procedure for future legislation. Commonwealth cases involving subordinate legislatures (e.g. Attorney-General for New South Wales v Trethowan [1932] AC 526) are used to support this but are distinguishable.
- Constitutional statutes cannot be impliedly repealed (Thoburn [2002]; HS2 [2014]).
- EU membership: under the European Communities Act 1972, courts disapplied Acts that conflicted with EU law (Factortame (No 2) [1991] 1 AC 603). This ended with Brexit, apart from the Windsor Framework in Northern Ireland (s7A EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018).
- R (Jackson) v Attorney General [2005] UKHL 56: the Hunting Act 2004 was passed under the Parliament Acts without the Lords' consent. Nine Law Lords held that the Parliament Act 1949, itself passed using the 1911 procedure, was valid, so the Hunting Act was valid; Acts passed under the Parliament Acts are primary legislation, not delegated legislation. In obiter remarks, Lord Steyn and Lord Hope treated parliamentary sovereignty as a creation of the common law. Lord Steyn suggested that the courts might not uphold legislation abolishing judicial review or the ordinary role of the courts; Lord Hope said sovereignty is "no longer, if it ever was, absolute" and that the rule of law enforced by the courts is the "ultimate controlling factor". Baroness Hale said the courts would treat with particular suspicion (and might even reject) an attempt to remove government action from all judicial scrutiny, and suggested that Parliament might redefine itself in ways that bind future Parliaments.
- R (Privacy International) v Investigatory Powers Tribunal [2019] UKSC 22: by a 4-3 majority, the Supreme Court held that an ouster clause in s67(8) of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 did not prevent judicial review of the Tribunal for errors of law. Lord Carnwath (for three justices, obiter) suggested that, under the rule of law, it is ultimately for the courts, not Parliament, to decide the limits of the power to exclude review.
- Parliament has responded with more carefully drafted ouster clauses, for example s2 of the Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 (excluding most judicial review of Upper Tribunal refusals of permission to appeal) and s3 of the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022.

Parliamentary accountability
The executive is accountable to Parliament through:
- the confidence convention;
- ministerial responsibility, questions and debates;
- select committees, whose chairs have been elected by the whole House since 2010, and the Public Accounts Committee;
- control of legislation and finance.

R (Miller) v Prime Minister; Cherry v Advocate General [2019] UKSC 41
The Prime Minister advised the Queen to prorogue Parliament for five weeks shortly before the Brexit deadline. A unanimous Supreme Court of 11 justices held:
- the issue was justiciable, because it concerned the legal limits of the prerogative power, not merely how it was exercised;
- those limits are set by fundamental principles: parliamentary sovereignty and parliamentary accountability;
- a decision to prorogue is unlawful if it has the effect of frustrating or preventing, without reasonable justification, Parliament's ability to carry out its constitutional functions as a legislature and as the body responsible for supervising the executive;
- no justification was offered, so the advice was unlawful, and the Order in Council was void: Parliament had not been prorogued.

Exam tips: Present the orthodox view clearly, then evaluate each challenge, distinguishing ratio from obiter (e.g. the Jackson and Privacy International remarks are obiter). Link accountability to Miller II, where the courts protected Parliament's role against the executive.

Judicial review allows the High Court (Administrative Court) to review the lawfulness of decisions by public bodies. It is not an appeal on the merits: the court asks whether the decision was lawfully made, not whether it was right.

Procedure
- Claims are brought under CPR Part 54 and s31 Senior Courts Act 1981, with permission, promptly and in any event within three months (CPR 54.5).
- Standing: the claimant must have a "sufficient interest" (s31(3)). The courts take a generous approach, including for pressure groups acting in the public interest (R v Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, ex p World Development Movement [1995] 1 WLR 386, the Pergau Dam case).
- Amenability: bodies exercising public functions, whether statutory or not (R v Panel on Take-overs and Mergers, ex p Datafin [1987] QB 815).
- Remedies (discretionary): quashing, prohibiting and mandatory orders, declarations and injunctions. Relief must be refused if it is highly likely the outcome would not have been substantially different (s31(2A)), although the court may still grant it if this is appropriate for reasons of exceptional public interest (s31(2B)); both were added by the Criminal Justice and Courts Act 2015.
- The Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 (s1) inserted s29A into the Senior Courts Act 1981, allowing suspended quashing orders and orders with limited or no retrospective effect. A proposed presumption in favour of using them was removed during the Bill's passage, so the court has discretion.

Grounds of review
Lord Diplock in Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service (GCHQ) [1985] AC 374 grouped the grounds into illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety, and suggested proportionality might be added.

Illegality
- Acting outside the powers conferred (ultra vires) or misunderstanding the law.
- Using power for an improper purpose, or frustrating the purpose of the Act (Padfield v Minister of Agriculture [1968] AC 997).
- Taking irrelevant considerations into account or ignoring relevant ones.
- Fettering discretion by applying a policy rigidly without being willing to consider exceptions (British Oxygen v Minister of Technology [1971] AC 610).
- Errors of law generally make a decision unlawful (Anisminic [1969]; R v Hull University Visitor, ex p Page [1993] AC 682).

Irrationality
- A decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it (Associated Provincial Picture Houses v Wednesbury Corporation [1948] 1 KB 223), or "so outrageous in its defiance of logic or of accepted moral standards" (GCHQ). Review is more intense where fundamental rights are at stake.

Proportionality
- Applies where Convention rights are engaged (R (Daly) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] UKHL 26). The four-stage test in Bank Mellat v HM Treasury (No 2) [2013] UKSC 39 asks whether the objective is important enough, whether the measure is rationally connected to it, whether a less intrusive measure could have been used, and whether a fair balance has been struck.

Procedural impropriety
- Fair hearing: Ridge v Baldwin [1964] AC 40 (a chief constable dismissed without a hearing). What fairness requires depends on context.
- Reasons: there is no general duty to give reasons, but fairness often requires them (R v Home Secretary, ex p Doody [1994] 1 AC 531).
- Consultation: if consultation takes place, it must be fair (R (Moseley) v Haringey LBC [2014] UKSC 56).
- Rule against bias: automatic disqualification where the decision-maker has an interest (R v Bow Street Magistrate, ex p Pinochet (No 2) [2000] 1 AC 119), and apparent bias where a fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real possibility of bias (Porter v Magill [2001] UKHL 67).
- Breach of statutory procedural requirements.

Legitimate expectation
- Procedural: a promise of a hearing or consultation must normally be honoured (Attorney-General of Hong Kong v Ng Yuen Shiu [1983] 2 AC 629).
- Substantive: a clear, unambiguous promise of a benefit may be enforced where going back on it would be so unfair as to be an abuse of power (R v North and East Devon Health Authority, ex p Coughlan [2001] QB 213, a promise of a "home for life").

Ouster clauses
Courts interpret ouster clauses narrowly (Anisminic; Privacy International), but Parliament can exclude review in clear terms, as in s11A of the Tribunals, Courts and Enforcement Act 2007 (inserted in 2022).

Exam tips: Deal in turn with amenability, standing, time, any ouster clause, each ground with authority, and remedies.

notes.h: The UK-EU constitutional relationship and Brexit
notes.body:
Membership: the European Communities Act 1972 (ECA)
- The UK joined the European Economic Community on 1 January 1973. The ECA gave EU law effect in domestic law: s2(1) made directly effective EU law part of UK law, and s2(4) required UK legislation to be read and take effect subject to it.
- The Court of Justice had developed the principles of direct effect (Van Gend en Loos, 1963) and primacy of EU law (Costa v ENEL, 1964).
- In R v Secretary of State for Transport, ex p Factortame (No 2) [1991] 1 AC 603, following a ruling of the Court of Justice, the House of Lords granted an interim injunction disapplying parts of the Merchant Shipping Act 1988 whose nationality conditions excluded Spanish-owned fishing vessels from the British register. Lord Bridge said that any limitation of sovereignty was accepted voluntarily by Parliament when it passed the ECA.
- In Macarthys v Smith [1979], Lord Denning suggested that if Parliament deliberately legislated to repudiate EU obligations, the courts would follow the later Act.
- In Thoburn [2002], Laws LJ explained EU supremacy as resting on the ECA, a constitutional statute, rather than on EU law itself. In HS2 [2014], the Supreme Court suggested EU law might not override other fundamental constitutional principles.

The referendum and Miller I
- The European Union Referendum Act 2015 provided for an advisory referendum, held on 23 June 2016, in which 51.9% voted to leave.
- R (Miller) v Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union [2017] UKSC 5: the Supreme Court held (8-3) that the government could not use the prerogative to give notice of withdrawal under Article 50 of the Treaty on European Union. Withdrawal would change domestic law and remove rights that Parliament had created through the ECA, which was a "conduit pipe" for EU law. An Act of Parliament was required. The court was unanimous that the Sewel convention was not legally enforceable.
- Parliament passed the European Union (Notification of Withdrawal) Act 2017.

Leaving the EU
- European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 (EUWA): repealed the ECA on exit day (31 January 2020) and created "retained EU law", preserving most EU-derived law as it stood at the end of the implementation period (11pm on 31 December 2020).
- European Union (Withdrawal Agreement) Act 2020: gave effect to the Withdrawal Agreement, including the Protocol on Ireland/Northern Ireland (now the Windsor Framework), and continued EU law during the implementation period. Section 7A of the EUWA gives the Withdrawal Agreement direct effect, which allowed the Protocol to modify the Acts of Union (Re Allister [2023] UKSC 5).
- European Union (Future Relationship) Act 2020: implemented the Trade and Cooperation Agreement.
- UK courts are no longer bound by Court of Justice decisions made after the implementation period, and the Supreme Court and some appellate courts may depart from retained EU case law.

The Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023
From the end of 2023:
- the principle of supremacy of EU law and the general principles of EU law ceased to apply in UK law;
- domestic legislation now takes priority over conflicting EU-derived law;
- retained EU law was renamed "assimilated law";
- a schedule of specified EU-derived instruments was revoked.

Constitutional impact of Brexit
- Parliamentary sovereignty in its orthodox form has largely been restored in relation to EU law: courts no longer disapply Acts for conflict with assimilated (formerly retained) EU law. The exception is the Windsor Framework: s7A EUWA requires every enactment to be read and have effect subject to the Withdrawal Agreement, so in May 2024 the High Court in Northern Ireland disapplied parts of the Illegal Migration Act 2023 there (In re NIHRC and JR295) for breaching Article 2 of the Windsor Framework. In Re Dillon [2026] UKSC 15 the Supreme Court read this route narrowly and set aside the Northern Ireland courts' disapplication of parts of the Legacy Act 2023, but the route itself remains.
- Devolution has been strained: the EUWA 2018 and later Acts were passed without devolved consent, showing the limits of the Sewel convention.
- Wide delegated powers to amend retained (now assimilated) law raise concerns about executive power.
- Northern Ireland has a special status under the Windsor Framework, including the Article 2 commitment that certain rights will not be diminished as a result of Brexit.

Exam tips: Explain the domestic legal basis for EU supremacy (the ECA), then show how Miller I, the EUWA 2018 and the 2023 Act changed it. Use Brexit as a case study of the courts' role, sovereignty and devolution.

notes.h: Human rights protection under the Human Rights Act 1998
notes.body:
The Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA), in force from 2 October 2000, gives effect in UK law to most rights in the European Convention on Human Rights (the "Convention rights"). It was designed to protect rights while preserving parliamentary sovereignty.

Key sections
- s2: courts must "take into account" judgments of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR).
- s3: so far as possible, legislation must be read and given effect compatibly with Convention rights; this does not affect the validity of incompatible primary legislation.
- s4: if that is impossible, the higher courts may declare the provision incompatible, which does not affect its validity, continuing operation or enforcement and does not bind the parties (s4(6)).
- s6: it is unlawful for a public authority to act incompatibly with Convention rights, unless primary legislation required it to act as it did (s6(2)). This includes courts and bodies with functions of a public nature (s6(3)), though not for their private acts (s6(5)).
- ss7-8: a "victim" can sue and may get just satisfaction; s10 allows remedial orders to amend incompatible legislation.
- s19: before Second Reading, the minister in charge of a Bill must state in writing that it is compatible (s19(1)(a)) or that, although he cannot say so, the government wishes the House to proceed (s19(1)(b)).

Section 2 and the "mirror principle"
In R (Ullah) v Special Adjudicator [2004] UKHL 26, Lord Bingham said courts should keep pace with Strasbourg: "no more, but certainly no less". Courts normally follow a clear and constant line of Strasbourg authority (Manchester City Council v Pinnock [2010] UKSC 45) but may occasionally decline (R v Horncastle [2009] UKSC 14), and should not generally go further than Strasbourg (R (AB) v Secretary of State for Justice [2021] UKSC 28). In June 2026, in a Northern Ireland devolution reference ([2026] UKSC 16), a unanimous seven-justice Supreme Court used the 1966 Practice Statement to overrule its own Article 5 decision in P v Cheshire West and Chester Council [2014] UKSC 19, holding that its "acid test" for deprivation of liberty misread the Strasbourg case law; the court cited Ullah and AB on keeping domestic law in line with Strasbourg.

Section 3 in practice
- Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza [2004] UKHL 30: "as his or her wife or husband" in the Rent Act 1977 was read to include a surviving same-sex partner. Section 3 can require departure from the ordinary meaning, but not a meaning inconsistent with a fundamental feature of the Act; it must "go with the grain".

Section 4 in practice
- Bellinger v Bellinger [2003] UKHL 21: the court refused to read "male" and "female" in the Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 to include a transgender woman, but declared incompatibility; Parliament passed the Gender Recognition Act 2004.
- A v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 56 (the Belmarsh case): indefinite detention of foreign terrorist suspects without trial was disproportionate and discriminatory; a declaration of incompatibility was made and the law was replaced.
- R (Nicklinson) v Ministry of Justice [2014] UKSC 38: the court declined to make a declaration about the ban on assisted suicide. A majority of the nine justices held that the court had the power to do so, but only Lady Hale and Lord Kerr would have made one; Lord Neuberger, Lord Mance and Lord Wilson thought it premature while Parliament considered the issue, and the other four saw it as a matter for Parliament.

Public authorities
Core public authorities (government departments, councils, police) are bound in everything they do; hybrid bodies only when performing public functions. In YL v Birmingham City Council [2007] UKHL 27 a private care home providing council-funded care was not performing a public function, a result Parliament later reversed (now Care Act 2014, s73).

Parliament and the HRA
- The Illegal Migration Act 2023 and the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024 were both introduced with s19(1)(b) statements. After the Supreme Court held that Rwanda was not then a safe country (R (AAA) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2023] UKSC 42), the 2024 Act required decision-makers to treat it as safe and disapplied key HRA provisions. The scheme was abandoned in 2024, and the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025 repealed the 2024 Act in full (s40) and most of the 2023 Act's operative provisions, including the duty to remove (s41), with effect from Royal Assent on 2 December 2025.
- At the time of writing (October 2026), a government Immigration and Asylum Bill, introduced in the Commons in June 2026 and proposing changes to how Article 8 is applied in immigration cases, was before Parliament; check its progress.

Exam tips: Ask whether a Convention right is engaged, whether the defendant is a public authority (s6), and, for legislation, whether it can be read compatibly (s3) or only declared incompatible (s4).

cards.b: Binding political rules that are not enforced by the courts (e.g. Royal Assent, ministerial responsibility, the Sewel convention). Courts may recognise but not enforce them (Miller I).
Laws LJ (obiter): 'constitutional statutes' cannot be impliedly repealed, only by express or specific words.
Obiter: 'constitutional instruments' exist, and EU law might not automatically override fundamental constitutional principles such as Article 9 of the Bill of Rights.
A search and seizure under a minister's warrant was unlawful because no law authorised it: public officials need legal authority to interfere with the person or property.
Parliament must use clear words to override fundamental rights; general or ambiguous words will not do so.
Employment tribunal fees were unlawful because they effectively prevented access to justice, a constitutional right protected by the common law.
The court would not enforce the convention of Cabinet confidentiality as such, but could restrain publication through the law of confidence; by then the Crossman diaries could be published.
Treaties bind the UK in international law but do not change domestic law unless Parliament incorporates them by statute.
Most public Bills can become law without the Lords' consent after about a year's delay (one month for money Bills); cannot be used to extend Parliament's life beyond five years.
Royal Assent 18 March 2026; removed the remaining 92 excepted hereditary peers from the end of the session on 29 April 2026; those with life peerages can still sit.
Ministers publicly support Cabinet decisions or resign; Cabinet discussions are confidential; a government that loses the confidence of the Commons must resign or seek dissolution.
The residue of discretionary common law powers of the Crown, mainly exercised by ministers (treaties, foreign affairs, armed forces, mercy, honours).

cards.f: A-G v De Keyser's Royal Hotel [1920]
cards.b: Where statute covers the same ground as a prerogative power, the prerogative is displaced and the statutory scheme must be used.

cards.f: R v Home Secretary, ex p Fire Brigades Union [1995]
cards.b: The Home Secretary could not use the prerogative to introduce a compensation scheme that frustrated a statutory scheme Parliament had enacted but not yet brought into force.
Prerogative powers are reviewable; whether a particular exercise is justiciable depends on its subject matter (national security here prevailed).

cards.f: Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022
cards.b: Repealed the Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011, revived the prerogative of dissolution, ousted the courts (s3) and provides for automatic dissolution five years after Parliament first meets (s4).
Devolution does not affect the power of the UK Parliament to make laws for Scotland.
Inserted by the Scotland Act 2016: the UK Parliament 'will not normally' legislate on devolved matters without the Scottish Parliament's consent. Not legally enforceable (Miller I).
A provision of an Act of the Scottish Parliament is not law if outside competence, e.g. it relates to reserved matters (Sch 5), breaches Sch 4 protections or is incompatible with Convention rights.

cards.f: AXA General Insurance v HM Advocate [2011]
cards.b: Acts of the Scottish Parliament are reviewable at common law only on extreme rule-of-law grounds, not irrationality.
Provisions of a Scottish Bill were outside competence because they would have restricted the UK Parliament's power to legislate for Scotland (modifying s28(7)).
A Bill for an advisory independence referendum related to the reserved matters of the Union and the UK Parliament, so it was outside competence.
96 members elected by closed-list proportional representation in 16 six-member constituencies, with four-year terms.
The Northern Ireland Protocol was lawfully implemented by the EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018, which modified the trade provisions of the Acts of Union 1800.
The Spirit of the Laws argued that liberty requires legislative, executive and judicial powers to be held by different bodies.
Ministers and others must uphold the continued independence of the judiciary and must not seek to influence particular judicial decisions through special access.
Lord Chief Justice head of judiciary (s7); Supreme Court created (s23, opened 2009); Judicial Appointments Commission (s61); s1 preserves the rule of law.
A minister can be held in contempt of court in his official capacity; injunctions can be granted against ministers.

cards.f: Dicey's three meanings of the rule of law (1885)
cards.b: No punishment except for breach of law proved in ordinary courts; equality of all, including officials, before the ordinary law; constitution as the result of judicial decisions on individual rights.

Eight principles including clear, accessible law; legal not discretionary decisions on rights; equality; officials acting within powers; protection of human rights; access to justice; fair trials; compliance with international law.

5-2: certificate invalid. Lord Neuberger (with Lords Kerr, Reed): s53 lacked the clear words needed to let the executive override a court merely by disagreeing. Lord Mance (with Lady Hale): override possible only with solid reasons, lacking here.
The Home Secretary's power to set murderers' minimum terms was incompatible with Article 6, as sentencing is a judicial function; declaration of incompatibility.
Parliament can make or unmake any law, and no person or body can override or set aside its legislation; Parliament cannot bind its successors.
Courts will not investigate whether Parliament followed its own procedures when passing an Act (enrolled Act rule).

cards.f: Ellen Street Estates v Minister of Health [1934]
cards.b: Parliament cannot bind its successors as to the form of later legislation; a later inconsistent Act impliedly repeals an earlier one.
The Parliament Act 1949 and the Hunting Act 2004 were valid; Parliament Acts legislation is primary. Obiter (Lords Steyn, Hope; Baroness Hale): possible limits on sovereignty.
4-3: s67(8) RIPA 2000 did not oust judicial review for errors of law. Obiter: courts ultimately decide the limits of ouster clauses under the rule of law.
Prorogation is unlawful if it frustrates or prevents, without reasonable justification, Parliament's ability to carry out its functions as legislature and supervisor of the executive.
The advice to prorogue was unlawful and the Order in Council void and of no effect; Parliament had not been prorogued.

cards.f: Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022, s2
cards.b: Inserted s11A into the Tribunals, Courts and Enforcement Act 2007, ousting most judicial review of Upper Tribunal refusals of permission to appeal (reversing Cart), with narrow exceptions such as bad faith.
Lord Diplock: illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety, with proportionality as a possible future ground.
A decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have come to it.
A minister's discretion must be used to promote, not frustrate, the policy and objects of the Act; refusing to refer a complaint for improper reasons was unlawful.
Is the objective sufficiently important? Is the measure rationally connected? Could a less intrusive measure have been used? Is there a fair balance?
Apparent bias: would a fair-minded and informed observer, having considered the facts, conclude there was a real possibility of bias?

cards.b: A clear promise of a 'home for life' created a substantive legitimate expectation; frustrating it was so unfair as to be an abuse of power.
Court must refuse relief if it is highly likely the outcome would not have been substantially different, but may still grant it for reasons of exceptional public interest (s31(2B)).
Allows suspended quashing orders and orders removing or limiting retrospective effect; the court has discretion, as the proposed presumption was dropped.

cards.b: s2(1) gave directly effective EU law effect in UK law; s2(4) required UK legislation to be read and take effect subject to it. Repealed on exit day by the EUWA 2018.
House of Lords disapplied parts of the Merchant Shipping Act 1988 by interim injunction to protect EU law rights; Lord Bridge: Parliament voluntarily accepted the limitation in 1972.
8-3: the prerogative could not be used to trigger Article 50, because withdrawal would change domestic law and remove statutory rights; an Act of Parliament was needed.
Created by the EUWA 2018: EU-derived law preserved as at 11pm on 31 December 2020. Renamed 'assimilated law' from the end of 2023.

cards.b: From the end of 2023: EU supremacy and general principles ceased to apply; domestic law prevails over EU-derived law; retained EU law renamed assimilated law.
Lord Denning: if Parliament deliberately passed an Act intending to repudiate EU obligations, the courts would follow the Act.
Gives the Withdrawal Agreement (including the Northern Ireland Protocol/Windsor Framework) effect in domestic law; upheld as modifying the Acts of Union in Re Allister [2023].

So far as possible, legislation must be read and given effect compatibly with Convention rights; does not affect the validity of incompatible primary legislation.
Higher courts may declare primary legislation incompatible; this does not affect its validity, continuing operation or enforcement and is not binding on the parties.
Before Second Reading, the minister must state in writing that the Bill is compatible (s19(1)(a)), or that he cannot say so but the government wishes to proceed (s19(1)(b)).

Unlawful for a public authority to act incompatibly with Convention rights, unless primary legislation required it (s6(2)); includes bodies with public functions (s6(3)(b)), but not their private acts.
Using s3, 'as his or her wife or husband' in the Rent Act 1977 was read to include same-sex partners; interpretation must go with the grain and not contradict a fundamental feature.
Domestic courts should keep pace with Strasbourg case law, 'no more, but certainly no less'; reaffirmed in R (AB) v SSJ [2021].
Indefinite detention of foreign terror suspects was disproportionate and discriminatory; declaration of incompatibility, and Parliament replaced the scheme.
