questions.q: Which statement about constitutional conventions is correct?
options: Conventions become legally enforceable when written into a statute that 'recognises' them, as with the Sewel convention
Conventions are enforced by the courts through judicial review
Conventions bind only the monarch, not ministers
Courts may recognise conventions but will not enforce them as law
questions.why: Miller I and Jonathan Cape show that courts can take conventions into account but do not enforce them. In Miller I the Supreme Court held that s28(8) of the Scotland Act 1998, which recognises the Sewel convention, did not turn it into a legal rule. Judicial review enforces legal limits, not conventions. Many conventions bind ministers, such as collective and individual ministerial responsibility.

questions.q: In R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor [2017], why was the Fees Order unlawful?
options: Because the Supreme Court declared it incompatible under s4 of the Human Rights Act 1998
Because fee-charging for courts and tribunals is always unlawful
Because the fees effectively prevented access to justice, which the common law protects as a constitutional right
Because it breached the Sewel convention
questions.why: The Supreme Court held that the fees were set at a level that prevented people from bringing claims, so the order was outside the powers conferred by the enabling Act, which had to be read consistently with the constitutional right of access to justice. The court did not say all fees are unlawful; it was the effect of these fees that mattered. The Sewel convention concerns legislating in devolved areas and was irrelevant. A s4 declaration applies to primary legislation, while the Fees Order was secondary legislation that could be quashed.

questions.q: Explain the idea of 'constitutional statutes' and assess its significance.
markScheme: Thoburn [2002]: Laws LJ's category; no implied repeal
Examples: Magna Carta, Bill of Rights, Acts of Union, HRA, devolution Acts
HS2 [2014]: constitutional instruments and possible hierarchy between them
Significance: qualifies Dicey's view that all Acts are equal; ties to common law constitutionalism
Limits: obiter, still subject to express repeal; uncertainty as to which statutes qualify
questions.modelAnswer:
In Thoburn v Sunderland CC [2002], Laws LJ argued that certain statutes are "constitutional" because they condition the legal relationship between citizen and state or enlarge or diminish fundamental rights. Examples include Magna Carta, the Bill of Rights 1689, the Acts of Union, the Human Rights Act 1998 and the devolution Acts. Unlike ordinary statutes, they cannot be impliedly repealed: a later Act repeals them only through express words or words so specific that Parliament's intention is clear. In HS2 [2014] Lords Neuberger and Mance went further, suggesting that some constitutional instruments might take priority over others, so that EU law under the European Communities Act might not override Article 9 of the Bill of Rights.

The idea matters because it qualifies the orthodox Diceyan view that every Act of Parliament has equal status and can be repealed by implication. It also reflects the growing role of the courts in identifying constitutional principles. However, both statements were obiter, there is no agreed test for which statutes qualify, and Parliament can still repeal constitutional statutes expressly. It is therefore a rule of interpretation rather than true entrenchment.

questions.q: Under the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022, which statement is correct?
options: An early general election requires a two-thirds majority in the Commons
Parliament is dissolved automatically five years after the day it first met, unless dissolved earlier
The courts may review a decision to dissolve Parliament for irrationality
The power to dissolve Parliament is now a statutory power exercised by the Speaker
questions.why: Section 4 provides for automatic dissolution at the fifth anniversary of the first meeting, and s2 revived the prerogative power to dissolve earlier. The two-thirds rule came from the repealed Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011. Section 3 expressly prevents courts from questioning dissolution decisions. The 2022 Act revived the prerogative, exercised by the monarch on the Prime Minister's request, rather than creating a statutory power for the Speaker.

questions.q: Parliament passes an Act creating a statutory compensation scheme, to be brought into force by the Home Secretary. He never commences it and instead introduces a less generous scheme under the prerogative. Following ex p Fire Brigades Union, what is the position?
options: Lawful, because decisions about commencing legislation are non-justiciable
Unlawful, because the prerogative can never be used where any statute exists
Unlawful, because the Home Secretary cannot use the prerogative to frustrate a scheme Parliament has enacted
Lawful, because the prerogative continues until a statute is in force
questions.why: The House of Lords held that, although the Home Secretary had discretion over when to commence the statutory scheme, he could not use the prerogative to introduce an inconsistent scheme that made the statutory one redundant. The idea that the prerogative carries on unaffected until commencement was the argument the majority rejected. Courts could review the decision because it related to the use of prerogative power against Parliament's will. The prerogative is displaced only where statute covers the same ground (De Keyser), not whenever any statute exists.

questions.q: What legal limits do the courts place on the royal prerogative?
markScheme: Cannot change the law of the land (Case of Proclamations; Miller I)
No new prerogatives (BBC v Johns)
Displaced by statute in the same field (De Keyser) and cannot frustrate statute (Fire Brigades Union)
Reviewable subject to justiciability (GCHQ); limits on prorogation (Miller II)
Statutory exclusions (e.g. s3 DCPA 2022)
questions.modelAnswer: The courts decide whether a prerogative power exists and what its limits are. The Case of Proclamations (1611) established that the Crown cannot change the law by proclamation, and Miller I [2017] confirmed that ministers cannot use the prerogative to change domestic law or remove rights Parliament has created, so notice of withdrawal from the EU needed an Act of Parliament. No new prerogatives can be created (BBC v Johns [1965]). Where Parliament legislates in the same area, the prerogative is displaced (De Keyser's Royal Hotel [1920]), and ministers cannot use it to frustrate the will of Parliament (Fire Brigades Union [1995]). Since GCHQ [1985], the exercise of prerogative powers is reviewable, though some subject matter, such as national security, is less suitable for review. In Miller II [2019] the Supreme Court held that a prorogation which, without reasonable justification, frustrated Parliament's ability to carry out its constitutional functions was unlawful. Parliament can also exclude review, as it has done for dissolution in s3 of the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022.

questions.q: The UK Parliament passes an Act on a devolved matter in Scotland after the Scottish Parliament has refused consent. What is the legal position?
options: The Act can be struck down by the Supreme Court for breaching the Sewel convention
The Act is valid; the Sewel convention is recognised in statute but is not legally enforceable
The Act is void because s28(8) of the Scotland Act 1998 requires consent
The Act is valid only once the Scottish Parliament later consents
questions.why: Miller I held that s28(8) recognises a political convention without creating a legal rule, and s28(7) preserves the UK Parliament's power to legislate for Scotland. Reading s28(8) as requiring consent is the argument the Supreme Court rejected. Validity does not depend on later consent. UK courts cannot strike down Acts of the UK Parliament, and in any event the convention is not legally enforceable.

questions.q: Why was the Scottish Independence Referendum Bill outside the Scottish Parliament's competence according to the Supreme Court in 2022?
options: Because the Scottish Parliament can never hold any referendum
Because a referendum would breach the Convention rights of voters
Because the referendum's result would have been legally binding
Because it related to reserved matters, the Union and the UK Parliament, even though the referendum would only be advisory
questions.why: The Supreme Court held that a provision relates to reserved matters if it has more than a loose or consequential connection with them, and an independence referendum would have important practical consequences for the Union and the UK Parliament even if only advisory. No Convention rights issue was decisive. The Bill was expressly advisory, so its legal effect was not the problem. The Scottish Parliament can hold referendums on devolved matters, so 'never' is wrong.

questions.q: Is the Scottish Parliament 'permanent'? Discuss with reference to the Scotland Act 2016 and case law.
markScheme: s63A Scotland Act 1998 (inserted 2016): permanence and referendum requirement
s28(7): UK Parliament's power preserved; parliamentary sovereignty
Miller I: Sewel convention not legally enforceable; s28(8) political
Can Parliament bind its successors? Manner and form debate; Jackson obiter
Conclusion: political permanence versus legal vulnerability
questions.modelAnswer: Section 63A of the Scotland Act 1998, inserted by the Scotland Act 2016, declares that the Scottish Parliament and Government are a permanent part of the UK's constitutional arrangements and will not be abolished except on the basis of a decision of the people of Scotland voting in a referendum. Politically, this is a strong commitment. Legally, however, s28(7) preserves the power of the UK Parliament to make laws for Scotland, and on the orthodox view of parliamentary sovereignty no Parliament can bind its successors, so a later Act could repeal s63A. In Miller I [2017] the Supreme Court held that the Sewel convention, recognised in s28(8), remained a political convention not enforceable in court, which suggests the courts would treat s63A in a similar way. Some argue that a "manner and form" requirement such as a referendum could bind Parliament, drawing on obiter remarks in Jackson [2005], but this is untested. The best conclusion is that the Scottish Parliament is politically entrenched but not legally permanent.

questions.q: According to Lord Neuberger's lead judgment (with which Lords Kerr and Reed agreed), why was the Attorney General's certificate invalid in R (Evans) v Attorney General [2015]?
options: Because s53 did not clearly allow the executive to override a judicial decision merely because it disagreed with it, which would offend the rule of law
Because the Freedom of Information Act 2000 does not allow ministers to issue certificates at all
Because the Human Rights Act 1998 required disclosure of the letters
Because the court has power to strike down primary legislation that offends the rule of law
questions.why: Lord Neuberger read s53 narrowly because overriding a court decision on mere disagreement conflicts with basic principles: judicial decisions bind and executive acts are reviewable. Lord Mance and Lady Hale reached the same result by a less strict route, so this reasoning is not that of the whole majority. Section 53 does allow certificates in some circumstances; the issue was the basis for this one. The HRA was not the ground of decision. The court did not strike down legislation; it interpreted s53 in line with constitutional principle.

questions.q: Which of these was a change made by the Constitutional Reform Act 2005?
options: The Lord Chief Justice became head of the judiciary of England and Wales
The Lord Chancellor became President of the Supreme Court
Judges were given power to strike down Acts of Parliament
The House of Lords Appellate Committee was given power to hear constitutional cases only
questions.why: Section 7 made the Lord Chief Justice head of the judiciary, removing that role from the Lord Chancellor. The Lord Chancellor lost judicial functions and has no role in the Supreme Court, which has its own President. The Act did not give judges power to strike down statutes. It abolished the Appellate Committee's judicial role by transferring it to the new Supreme Court.

questions.q: To what extent does the UK constitution observe the separation of powers?
markScheme: Defines the doctrine (Montesquieu) and pure v partial versions
Fusion of executive and legislature: ministers in Parliament, government majority
Judicial independence: CRA 2005 (ss1, 3, 7, 23, 61)
Checks and balances: judicial review (M v Home Office, Fire Brigades Union, Miller II), parliamentary scrutiny
Judges and Parliament: Duport Steels; Anderson
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The separation of powers, associated with Montesquieu, requires the legislative, executive and judicial functions to be held by separate bodies so that power is not concentrated. A pure separation is not found in the UK. The executive and legislature are fused: ministers must sit in Parliament, and a government with a Commons majority largely controls the legislative agenda. Bagehot called this near fusion of executive and legislative power the "efficient secret" of the constitution.

The judiciary, by contrast, is now formally separate. The Constitutional Reform Act 2005 made the Lord Chief Justice head of the judiciary (s7), removed the Lord Chancellor's judicial role, created the Supreme Court outside Parliament (s23), set up the Judicial Appointments Commission (s61) and required ministers to uphold judicial independence (s3). Before 2009 the highest court sat as a committee of the House of Lords.

The UK relies more on checks and balances. Courts restrain the executive through judicial review (Fire Brigades Union [1995]; M v Home Office [1994]; Miller II [2019]), while respecting Parliament's role in making law (Duport Steels v Sirs [1980]). Sentencing has been treated as a judicial function (Anderson [2002]). Parliament scrutinises ministers through questions and select committees. Overall, the UK observes a partial separation centred on judicial independence, with weak separation between executive and legislature.

questions.q: In R (Jackson) v Attorney General [2005], what did the House of Lords decide as part of its ratio?
options: The Parliament Act 1949 and the Hunting Act 2004 were valid
Parliament is no longer sovereign after the European Communities Act 1972
The courts have power to strike down Acts that abolish judicial review
Acts passed under the Parliament Acts are delegated legislation and can be reviewed
questions.why: The decision was that the 1949 Act, and therefore the Hunting Act, was valid, and that legislation under the Parliament Acts is primary legislation. The suggestion that courts might refuse to uphold an Act abolishing judicial review was obiter (chiefly Lord Steyn, with related remarks by Lord Hope and Baroness Hale), not ratio. The appellants' argument that Parliament Acts legislation is delegated was rejected. The case was not about the European Communities Act.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the decision in R (Miller) v Prime Minister [2019]?
options: The Supreme Court held that the advice to prorogue was unlawful because it frustrated Parliament's functions without reasonable justification, and the prorogation was void
The Supreme Court held that it could not review prorogation because it is a prerogative power
The Supreme Court held that the advice was lawful but politically improper
The Supreme Court ordered Parliament to be recalled under the Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011
questions.why: The unanimous court treated the case as about the legal limits of the prerogative, found no justification for a five-week prorogation, and held the Order in Council void. The court rejected the argument that the matter was non-justiciable. It found the advice unlawful, not merely improper. The 2011 Act did not govern prorogation, and the court did not need to order a recall because Parliament had never been prorogued.

questions.q: Explain the significance of R (Privacy International) v Investigatory Powers Tribunal [2019] for parliamentary sovereignty.
markScheme: Facts: s67(8) RIPA 2000 ouster ('shall not be ... liable to be questioned in any court')
Majority (4-3) held it did not exclude review for errors of law; Anisminic reasoning on 'determination'
Lord Carnwath's obiter: courts ultimately determine limits of ouster under the rule of law
Dissents (Lords Reed, Wilson, Sumption): Parliament's clear intention should be respected
Significance: common law constitutionalism v orthodox sovereignty; Parliament's response (JRCA 2022 s2)
questions.modelAnswer:
Section 67(8) of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 provided that decisions of the Investigatory Powers Tribunal "shall not be subject to appeal or be liable to be questioned in any court". Privacy International sought judicial review of the Tribunal's ruling on a point of law. By a 4-3 majority the Supreme Court held that the clause did not exclude review for errors of law. Following Anisminic, a decision affected by an error of law was not a true "determination" protected by the clause, and Parliament had not used sufficiently clear words to exclude review.

The case is significant because Lord Carnwath, with Lady Hale and Lord Kerr, suggested obiter that it is ultimately for the courts, applying the rule of law, to decide how far Parliament can exclude review, and that a clause purporting to exclude review of errors of law by a tribunal of limited jurisdiction might not be upheld. This challenges Dicey's view that Parliament's enactments cannot be questioned. The dissenting justices (Lords Reed, Wilson and Sumption) argued that the words were clear and should be respected. Parliament's later drafting, for example s2 of the Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022, shows it now writes ouster clauses with this case in mind. The decision therefore sharpens the tension between common law constitutionalism and parliamentary sovereignty, though the challenge remains obiter.

questions.q: A council adopts a policy that it will never grant licences to street traders under 21, and refuses Zoe's application without looking at her circumstances. Which ground of review is most clearly engaged?
options: Apparent bias, because the council has prejudged applications
Breach of a substantive legitimate expectation
Irrationality, because any age-based policy is outrageous
Illegality, by unlawfully fettering its discretion through rigid application of a policy
questions.why: British Oxygen allows authorities to have policies but requires them to remain willing to consider exceptions; refusing to consider Zoe's case at all fetters the discretion. Bias concerns the decision-maker's interests or relationships, not a general policy. No promise was made to Zoe, so legitimate expectation does not arise. An age threshold is not necessarily irrational; the problem is its rigid application.

questions.q: A minister makes a decision after a consultation that failed to tell consultees about realistic alternatives. The court finds the process unlawful but is satisfied it is highly likely the decision would have been the same. What must the court usually do?
options: Refuse relief under s31(2A) Senior Courts Act 1981, unless there is an exceptional public interest in granting it
Award damages to every consultee
Issue a declaration of incompatibility
Quash the decision, because any procedural error makes a decision void
questions.why: Section 31(2A) requires the court to refuse relief where it is highly likely the outcome would not have been substantially different, subject to the exceptional public interest exception. The idea that every procedural error leads to quashing ignores both s31(2A) and the court's general discretion over remedies. Damages are rarely available in judicial review and are not a general remedy for procedural unfairness. Declarations of incompatibility apply to legislation under the Human Rights Act, not to unfair consultation.

questions.q: Explain the doctrine of substantive legitimate expectation with reference to ex p Coughlan.
markScheme: Distinguishes procedural and substantive legitimate expectations (Ng Yuen Shiu)
Requirements: clear, unambiguous, unqualified representation by the decision-maker
Coughlan facts: 'home for life' promise to a small group
Test: frustrating the expectation so unfair as to be an abuse of power; court weighs overriding public interest
Comment on tension with discretion/policy change
questions.modelAnswer: A legitimate expectation arises when a public body, by a promise or established practice, leads a person to expect a particular procedure or outcome. A procedural expectation, such as a promise of consultation, will normally be enforced (A-G of Hong Kong v Ng Yuen Shiu [1983]). A substantive expectation concerns a benefit itself. In R v North and East Devon Health Authority, ex p Coughlan [2001], Miss Coughlan, who was severely disabled, moved to a new care home after the health authority promised the residents it would be their "home for life". The authority later decided to close it. The Court of Appeal held that the promise created a substantive legitimate expectation. The representation was clear and made to a small group, and frustrating it would be so unfair as to amount to an abuse of power, since no overriding public interest justified the closure. The decision was quashed. The doctrine is controversial because it constrains public bodies' freedom to change policy, so the courts require a clear, unambiguous and unqualified promise and weigh any overriding public interest.

questions.q: What was the main reason the Supreme Court gave in Miller I [2017] for requiring an Act of Parliament before notice under Article 50 could be given?
options: Because the Sewel convention required the consent of the devolved legislatures
Because treaty-making powers can never be exercised by the prerogative
Because withdrawal would change domestic law and remove rights created by Parliament, which the prerogative cannot do
Because the referendum result was legally binding on the government
questions.why: The majority held that the ECA made EU law a source of domestic law, so withdrawal would alter UK law and remove statutory rights, which requires Parliament. The referendum was advisory under the 2015 Act. The court unanimously held the Sewel convention unenforceable. Making and withdrawing from treaties is normally a prerogative power; the issue was the domestic legal effect of this particular withdrawal.

questions.q: After the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023, what happens if a provision of assimilated law (formerly retained EU law) conflicts with an Act of Parliament passed in 2010?
options: The courts must refer the question to the Court of Justice of the EU
The Act of Parliament prevails, because EU supremacy no longer applies and domestic legislation takes priority
The courts must declare the Act incompatible under the Human Rights Act 1998
The assimilated law prevails because EU-derived law retains supremacy over pre-2020 legislation
questions.why: From the end of 2023 the 2023 Act abolished the supremacy principle for all domestic legislation, whenever made, and introduced a priority rule in favour of domestic legislation. Supremacy over pre-2021 legislation applied only under the original EUWA s5 and was abolished by the 2023 Act. UK courts cannot refer questions to the Court of Justice on assimilated law. A declaration of incompatibility concerns Convention rights, not EU-derived law.

questions.q: How did the courts reconcile EU membership with parliamentary sovereignty, and what has changed since Brexit?
markScheme: ECA 1972 s2(1), (4); primacy (Costa v ENEL)
Factortame (No 2): disapplication; Lord Bridge's 'voluntary' limitation
Thoburn/HS2: supremacy based on domestic statute; constitutional statutes
Miller I: ECA as conduit pipe; Parliament needed for withdrawal
EUWA 2018 and REUL Act 2023: end of supremacy, assimilated law
Evaluation: orthodox sovereignty largely restored (Windsor Framework/s7A exception), but legacy of common law constitutionalism
questions.modelAnswer:
While the UK was a member, EU law took effect through the European Communities Act 1972, which gave directly effective EU law force in the UK (s2(1)) and required later Acts to take effect subject to it (s2(4)). In Factortame (No 2) [1991] the House of Lords disapplied parts of the Merchant Shipping Act 1988 that conflicted with EU law. Lord Bridge reconciled this with sovereignty by saying Parliament had voluntarily accepted the limitation in 1972. In Thoburn [2002], Laws LJ said EU supremacy rested on the ECA as a constitutional statute, which could not be impliedly repealed, and the Supreme Court in HS2 [2014] suggested EU law might not override fundamental constitutional principles. The courts therefore treated supremacy as a domestic choice that Parliament could reverse, a view consistent with Miller I [2017], where the ECA was a "conduit pipe" that only Parliament could close.

After Brexit, the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 repealed the ECA and preserved EU-derived law as retained EU law, initially with supremacy over pre-2021 legislation. The Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 abolished supremacy and the general principles from the end of 2023 and renamed the body of law "assimilated law". Orthodox sovereignty has therefore largely been restored as regards EU law. The main exception is the Windsor Framework: under s7A EUWA, enactments take effect subject to the Withdrawal Agreement, and in 2024 the Northern Ireland High Court disapplied parts of the Illegal Migration Act 2023 in Northern Ireland on that basis, although the Supreme Court read this route narrowly in Re Dillon [2026] UKSC 15. More generally, the case law on constitutional statutes and common law rights developed during membership remains influential.

questions.q: A court cannot read a provision of an Act compatibly with Article 8 under s3 HRA, and makes a declaration of incompatibility under s4. What is the legal effect?
options: The government must amend the provision within six months
The provision is void from the date of the declaration
The provision continues in force and must still be applied; it is for Parliament or a minister (by remedial order) to respond
The provision is suspended until Parliament amends it
questions.why: Section 4(6) provides that a declaration does not affect the validity, continuing operation or enforcement of the provision, and the response is political, by Parliament or through a s10 remedial order. The court has no power to make an Act void. There is no suspension power under s4. No legal deadline obliges the government to amend, although in practice governments usually respond.

questions.q: In Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza [2004], what limit on s3 HRA did the House of Lords identify?
options: Section 3 can be used only by the Supreme Court
Section 3 cannot be used where the statutory words are clear and unambiguous
Section 3 applies only to legislation passed after the HRA came into force
Section 3 cannot be used to adopt a meaning inconsistent with a fundamental feature of the legislation
questions.why: Ghaidan held that s3 can require a court to depart from the unambiguous meaning of words, but the interpretation must go with the grain of the legislation and not contradict a fundamental feature. The idea that clear words cannot be reinterpreted was rejected: s3 is not limited to ambiguity. Section 3 applies to legislation 'whenever enacted' (s3(2)(a)). All courts must apply s3; only s4 declarations are limited to higher courts.

questions.q: How does the Human Rights Act 1998 protect rights while preserving parliamentary sovereignty?
markScheme: s3 strong interpretive obligation (Ghaidan) but does not affect validity
s4 declarations: no effect on validity; political response (Bellinger, Belmarsh)
s6(2): public authority acting under incompatible primary legislation does not act unlawfully
s19 statements and s10 remedial orders; Parliament's ability to legislate incompatibly (s19(1)(b), Safety of Rwanda Act)
Evaluation: 'dialogue' model; strong de facto influence; criticism from both sides
questions.modelAnswer: The HRA gives Convention rights domestic effect without allowing courts to strike down Acts of Parliament. Section 3 requires courts to read legislation compatibly "so far as it is possible", which can be a strong obligation: in Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza [2004] the Rent Act was read to include same-sex partners. But s3 does not affect the validity of incompatible primary legislation, and courts cannot adopt an interpretation that contradicts a fundamental feature of the Act. Where compatible interpretation is impossible, the higher courts can make a declaration of incompatibility under s4, which does not affect the validity, continuing operation or enforcement of the provision. The response is left to Parliament, as when it passed the Gender Recognition Act 2004 after Bellinger and replaced the Belmarsh detention scheme. Section 6(2) protects public authorities that act incompatibly because primary legislation required them to. Section 19 requires ministers to say whether Bills are compatible, but Parliament can still proceed with a s19(1)(b) statement, as with the Illegal Migration Act 2023 and the Safety of Rwanda Act 2024 (both since repealed wholly or largely by the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025). The model is often described as a "dialogue" between courts and Parliament. In practice governments almost always respond to declarations, giving the courts real influence, which some see as too much and others as too little protection.

questions.q: Essay. 'After Jackson, Privacy International and the two Miller cases, the orthodox Diceyan account of parliamentary sovereignty no longer describes the UK constitution.' Discuss.
markScheme: States the Diceyan orthodoxy: unlimited legislative competence, no body can set aside an Act, Parliament cannot bind successors (Pickin; Ellen Street Estates)
Jackson [2005]: ratio (1949 Act valid; Parliament Acts legislation primary) versus obiter on limits (Lords Steyn, Hope; Baroness Hale)
Privacy International [2019]: narrow reading of ouster; Lord Carnwath's obiter; dissents
Miller I [2017]: protects Parliament's role against prerogative (supports sovereignty)
Miller II [2019]: parliamentary sovereignty and accountability as limits on prerogative; void prorogation
Context: constitutional statutes (Thoburn, HS2), Brexit largely restoring orthodox position (REUL Act 2023), with the Windsor Framework/s7A EUWA exception, devolution and Sewel
Parliament's responses (JRCA 2022 s2, DCPA 2022 s3) showing continued legislative supremacy
Balanced conclusion distinguishing legal theory from practice and ratio from obiter
questions.modelAnswer:
Dicey's orthodox account holds that Parliament can make or unmake any law, that no person or body can set aside an Act of Parliament, and that Parliament cannot bind its successors. Courts do not inquire into how an Act was passed (Pickin) and later Acts impliedly repeal earlier ones (Ellen Street Estates). The question is whether recent cases have changed this.

Jackson [2005] upheld the validity of the Parliament Act 1949 and the Hunting Act 2004, which is consistent with orthodoxy: the court treated Parliament Acts legislation as primary legislation. However, Lord Steyn and Lord Hope treated sovereignty as a common law construct, Lord Steyn suggested that courts might not uphold an Act abolishing judicial review, and Baroness Hale suggested Parliament might redefine itself. These remarks were obiter, but they show senior judges contemplating limits.

Privacy International [2019] went further in practice. The majority read an apparently clear ouster clause as not excluding review for errors of law, and Lord Carnwath suggested (obiter) that courts ultimately decide the limits of ouster clauses under the rule of law. Three justices dissented, emphasising respect for Parliament's words.

The Miller cases are different. Miller I [2017] protected Parliament against the executive: the prerogative could not be used to remove statutory rights. Miller II [2019] held prorogation unlawful because it frustrated Parliament's ability to legislate and hold the government to account, relying on parliamentary sovereignty and accountability as constitutional principles. These decisions strengthen Parliament's position, so they are better seen as applications of sovereignty than challenges to it.

Other developments point both ways. Constitutional statutes (Thoburn, HS2) qualify implied repeal. On the other hand, Brexit has largely restored the orthodox position as regards EU law: since the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023, assimilated EU-derived law no longer prevails over Acts of Parliament. The one significant exception is the Windsor Framework, which s7A of the EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018 gives priority over other enactments in Northern Ireland; but that priority itself rests on an Act of Parliament, and the Supreme Court construed it narrowly in Re Dillon [2026] UKSC 15. Parliament has also shown its continuing supremacy by drafting stronger ouster clauses, such as s2 of the Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 and s3 of the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022, and by legislating on devolved matters without consent, which Miller I confirmed was legally possible.

In conclusion, the Diceyan account remains legally accurate in its core: outside the Windsor Framework (where disapplication rests on Parliament's own choice in s7A), no court has refused to apply an Act of Parliament since Brexit, and the most radical statements about limits on Parliament are obiter. But it no longer fully describes the constitution, because the courts now read statutes against strong common law principles and protect Parliament's role against the executive. Sovereignty is best understood as operating within a framework of constitutional principles that the courts help to define.

questions.q: Problem question. The (fictional) Community Arts Funding Act 2025 gives the Secretary of State power to award grants 'to promote access to the arts in deprived areas', and provides that 'no decision under this Act shall be questioned in any legal proceedings whatsoever'. In January, the department wrote to Northside Theatre, a charity in a deprived area, promising that it would be consulted before any change to its annual grant. In March, the Secretary of State cut Northside's grant to zero without consultation, saying privately that the theatre had staged a play mocking the government. The same month she awarded a large grant to a theatre in a wealthy area whose chair is her brother. Advise Northside Theatre on whether it can challenge these decisions by judicial review, and on likely remedies.
markScheme: Procedure: amenability (statutory power), standing (sufficient interest; Northside directly affected), time limit (promptly and within three months), permission
Ouster clause: narrow interpretation (Anisminic; Privacy International); decisions affected by error of law not protected 'decisions'; contrast clearly drafted ousters (JRCA 2022 s2)
Illegality: improper purpose/irrelevant considerations (Padfield); grant to wealthy area frustrates statutory purpose
Procedural impropriety: procedural legitimate expectation from promise of consultation (Ng Yuen Shiu); fair consultation (Moseley)
Bias: brother as chair; automatic disqualification or apparent bias (Pinochet (No 2); Porter v Magill)
Irrationality as alternative (Wednesbury); possible Article 10 point if HRA engaged and proportionality
Remedies: quashing order, mandatory/declaration; s31(2A) and s29A suspended quashing orders; discretion
Clear conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Preliminary issues. The Secretary of State is exercising a statutory power, so her decisions are amenable to judicial review. Northside, as the theatre whose grant was cut, plainly has a sufficient interest (s31(3) Senior Courts Act 1981). It must act promptly and in any event within three months of the March decisions (CPR 54.5) and obtain permission.

The ouster clause. The Act says no decision "shall be questioned in any legal proceedings whatsoever". Courts read such clauses narrowly. In Anisminic the House of Lords held that a decision tainted by an error of law is not a "determination" protected by an ouster clause, and in Privacy International [2019] the Supreme Court applied this to a similar clause, with three justices suggesting obiter that the courts ultimately decide how far review can be excluded. Unlike s11A of the Tribunals, Courts and Enforcement Act 2007, this clause does not expressly cover decisions made in error of law or "purported" decisions. A court is likely to hold that it does not prevent review of unlawful decisions.

Illegality. The power exists to promote access to the arts in deprived areas. Cutting a grant because a play mocked the government is using the power for an improper purpose and taking an irrelevant consideration into account, like the minister in Padfield, who could not use his discretion to frustrate the Act's purpose. Awarding a large grant to a theatre in a wealthy area also appears to fall outside the statutory purpose. If the Human Rights Act applies, the cut may also be a disproportionate interference with freedom of expression (Article 10), but the improper purpose argument is strong without it.

Procedural impropriety. The January letter was a clear promise of consultation, creating a procedural legitimate expectation that should be honoured unless there is an overriding public interest (A-G of Hong Kong v Ng Yuen Shiu). No consultation took place, so the decision is procedurally unfair.

Bias. The grant to the theatre chaired by the Secretary of State's brother raises apparent bias: a fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real possibility of bias (Porter v Magill). Northside could challenge the award if it has standing (for example, if the grants come from the same limited fund).

Irrationality. As an alternative, cutting the grant to zero for these reasons may be so unreasonable that no reasonable minister could have done it (Wednesbury).

Remedies. Remedies are discretionary. Northside should seek a quashing order of the cut and, perhaps, a mandatory order requiring a fresh decision after consultation. Section 31(2A) is unlikely to bar relief, because it cannot be said that the outcome would highly likely have been the same without the improper motive. The court could use its power under s29A to suspend a quashing order, for example to avoid disrupting other grants, but here prompt relief seems appropriate.

Conclusion. Despite the ouster clause, Northside has strong grounds of illegality and procedural unfairness, and a quashing order is likely.
